passage: The hostel's wifi crawled, and Rashmi's phone showed one bar when Jeevan's message arrived: "WORST DAY EVER!!!!!!! 😭😭 I HATE EVERYTHING". She read it twice. Jeevan often wrote like that, once in capitals over a burnt toast, yet last week he had truly been stressed about his practical exam. With the signal cutting in and out, she couldn't hear his voice or see his face, so she couldn't tell which Jeevan had typed it. She walked to the corridor window, where the network was better, and called. "Hey, is this a play worst day or a real worst day?" He laughed. "Bit of both. I missed the bus, and the exam thing is still bugging me. Thanks for asking though."

qa.q: How many bars of signal did Rashmi's phone show?
qa.a: Her phone showed one bar.

qa.q: What was Rashmi worried about when she read Jeevan's message?
qa.a: She wasn't sure if the capitals and dramatic emojis were play or real distress, since Jeevan usually exaggerated but had been stressed about his practical exam.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do that helped?
qa.a: She checked directly by calling and asking whether it was play or real, instead of guessing from the capitals.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see his own message?
qa.a: He may see it as half joke and half honest stress, and he may not realise how it looks from far away with no face or voice to read.

grounding: A teen writes in capitals with many exclamation marks and dramatic emojis, which may be play or real intensity, and a quick check helps.

passage: Himani posted a story that evening: "I CANNOT BELIEVE THIS!!!!!! 😱 my life is a disaster." Under it was a photo of her test paper. Within minutes people were reacting with laughing faces and "same!!". Pallavi, sitting in her own room, wasn't sure what to think. Himani had a habit of dramatic posts for her followers, and she also had a real habit of caring too much about marks. Pallavi typed a private message instead of joining the reactions: "Hey, is that a joke-dramatic or a really-upset one? I'm around either way." Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. Then: "Honestly, a little of both. I'll call you in ten minutes." Pallavi put the phone down, relieved she'd asked.

qa.q: What did Himani's story show under the caption?
qa.a: It showed a photo of her test paper.

qa.q: What might Himani be feeling when she posts the story?
qa.a: Probably a mix of real upset about the marks and a wish to be seen and joined by her followers, and she admits it is a little of both.

qa.q: Why was a private message better than adding a reaction?
qa.a: The public reactions treated the post as a joke, while a private check gave Himani room to say if some of it was real.

qa.q: How might the followers have read the post differently from Pallavi?
qa.a: They only saw capitals and an emoji and took it as playful, while Pallavi knew Himani's habits and worried about the real feeling under it.

grounding: A teen's capitals and dramatic emoji may be play, real intensity or performing for followers, and a quick private check helps.

passage:
"Preeti, did you see your own post? 'I'M LITERALLY DYING!!! THIS MATHS TEST HAS DESTROYED MY WHOLE EXISTENCE 😭'"
Preeti laughed, spinning on the library chair. "Yeah? So?"
Mridul put his bag down. "So I was a bit worried. You've been stressed all week."
"Mridul. It's a joke. Everyone posts like that."
"Okay. I just couldn't tell from the capitals."
She stopped spinning. "Honestly? Half joke."
"And the other half?"
"The other half is I think I got question four completely wrong, and my mother's going to ask about it tonight."
"That's a real thing."
"It's a small real thing. The 'destroyed my existence' part is for the likes." She grinned. "But thanks for checking. Most people just put a laughing face."
"Want to look at question four together?"
"Yes. Please. Before my existence is actually destroyed."

qa.q: Which question did Preeti think she got wrong?
qa.a: Question four.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling behind the dramatic post?
qa.a: Preeti felt partly playful and partly worried, genuinely stressed about question four and her mother's questions, while exaggerating for likes.

qa.q: What did Mridul's quick check achieve?
qa.a: It separated the playful exaggeration from the real worry, so he could offer help with question four.

qa.q: How might most of Preeti's followers have read the post?
qa.a: They probably read it as a funny, dramatic joke and reacted with laughing faces, missing the small real worry.

grounding: The dialogue shows an exaggerated online post mixing play and real feeling, and a friend's quick check clarifying it.

passage:
Last spring I posted "WORST DAY OF MY LIFE!!!!!" with three broken-heart emojis. What actually happened: I dropped my ice cream on the way home. That's it.
I didn't even feel that bad. But I'd noticed that dramatic posts got way more comments. People asked "what happened??" and I liked that.
Then Gopika messaged me privately: "Hey. Just checking you're okay? You don't have to say what it is."
I felt awful. She was actually worried. I'd been performing for followers and a real friend thought something terrible had happened.
I wrote back, "Oh no, it was ice cream. I'm fine. Sorry for scaring you."
She sent a laughing face and said, "Good. But if it's ever real, tell me."
Now I try to make my posts match my actual mood. Mostly. Sometimes the ice cream really does deserve capitals.
- Pema

qa.q: What actually happened on Pema's "worst day"?
qa.a: Pema dropped an ice cream on the way home.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling after reading Gopika's message?
qa.a: Pema felt guilty and embarrassed, realising the performance for followers had genuinely worried a real friend.

qa.q: What did Gopika do well when she saw the post?
qa.a: Gopika checked privately and gently, without demanding details, and offered support if it was ever real.

qa.q: How did the post look to Gopika compared with Pema's real mood?
qa.a: To Gopika it looked like real distress, while Pema was only mildly annoyed and exaggerating for attention.

grounding: The account shows capitals and dramatic emojis used to perform for followers, and a friend's quick check revealing the real mood.

passage:
Teacher's note - Vinita, Class 10 class teacher, Monday
At 11 last night Lokesh posted in the class group: "I CAN'T DO THIS ANYMORE!!!! 😤😤" A few students replied with laughing faces. Others replied "same bro."
I couldn't tell whether this was play, frustration or something more serious. Capitals and exclamation marks can mean any of these.
So this morning, before first period, I asked him quietly to walk with me to the staff room. "I saw your post last night. How are you really?"
He laughed, then stopped. "It's the science project. My partner hasn't done anything, and it's due Friday. I was so angry I couldn't sleep."
I asked whether he was feeling unsafe or just very stressed. He said, clearly, "Just stressed, Ma'am. I promise."
I've spoken to his partner, and we've set a check-in for Wednesday. I also told Lokesh my door is open anytime.

qa.q: When is the science project due?
qa.a: It's due Friday.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he wrote the post?
qa.a: Lokesh was angry and stressed about his partner doing nothing, frustrated enough to lose sleep, but not in danger.

qa.q: Why was Vinita's quick check wise?
qa.a: Because capitals and exclamation marks could mean play, frustration or something serious, so asking privately found the real meaning and let her help.

qa.q: How did the classmates who replied "same bro" read the post?
qa.a: They probably read it as the usual dramatic complaining, not stopping to check what Lokesh really felt.

grounding: The teacher's note shows an intense online post being hard to read and a quick, private check clarifying the real feeling.

passage:
Friday
At 7:40 this morning Keerthana posted: "I AM LITERALLY DYING!!!!!! WORST DAY OF MY ENTIRE LIFE" with three crying faces and a skull. My heart jumped. Keerthana's grandmother has been ill, so for about ten seconds I was really scared. Then I remembered she also wrote "I AM DEAD" when the canteen ran out of chilli potatoes. Still. I messaged her privately: "hey, actual dying or canteen dying? 🙂" She replied, "CANTEEN LEVEL. I spilled ink on my white uniform on the bus. Everyone saw 😩" Then a second message: "thanks for checking tho Pema. Nani's okay, she's home now." So maybe 20 percent real feeling and 80 percent show for the class group. I do this too. Last week I wrote "BEST DAY EVER!!!" about a samosa. Maybe typing needs a volume knob. Taking my spare cardigan to school tomorrow in case the ink hasn't come out.

qa.q: What did Keerthana spill on her uniform?
qa.a: Keerthana spilled ink on her white uniform on the bus.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when the 7:40 post appeared?
qa.a: Pema felt a jolt of fear, knowing Keerthana's grandmother had been ill, before remembering how often Keerthana exaggerates; the worry was real for those ten seconds.

qa.q: What small step helped Pema read the post right?
qa.a: A quick private check, 'actual dying or canteen dying?', got the real meaning in one reply instead of guessing from capitals and emojis. 🙂

qa.q: How much of the post was real feeling for Keerthana?
qa.a: The ink was genuinely embarrassing for Keerthana, but the capitals and emojis were mostly performance for the class group, as 'CANTEEN LEVEL' shows.

grounding: It shows capital letters and dramatic emojis mixing real feeling with performance online, and a quick private check clarifying the tone.
